title: Deadline and Protocol
premise: Jonah Oyelaran, a deniable fixer for a diplomatic mission that exists on no official registry, is summoned when his own voiceprint unlocks a black server in Lagos containing evidence of an imminent attack designed to look like an industrial accident. The trail implicates the very agency that created him, forcing him to partner with Amara, the analyst who betrayed his location to save her brother. As dawn and the extraction flight approach, Jonah must choose between burning the protocol that protects him or letting the attack proceed. He stops the attack at the cost of his own cover, exposing the agency and walking away with Amara into an unwitnessed life.
about_author: Felix Thornbury is the pen name of a former policy analyst who spent a decade drafting cables he was never allowed to sign. He writes thrillers about the people who do the work history refuses to record.

chapters.title: The Voice That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. A routine document burn in Vienna is interrupted when Jonah's own voiceprint unlocks a server in Lagos he's never touched. Inside: schematics for a refinery 'accident' scheduled in forty hours. The beat is cold dread — the machinery he serves has just spoken in his voice without permission.

chapters.title: Deniable Men
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. His handler, Voss, orders him to stand down; the case belongs to someone else now. Jonah disobeys, pulling the server's access logs and finding Amara Sekoni's credentials — an analyst who flagged the plot weeks ago and was silenced. Beat: stubborn loyalty curdling into suspicion of everyone above him.

chapters.title: Amara
chapters.summary: POV: Amara. In Lagos, Amara watches Jonah break into her flat and doesn't shoot him. She reveals her brother is being held as leverage to keep her quiet, and the 'accident' will kill three hundred workers to trigger an insurance windfall. Beat: two liars recognizing each other's exhaustion.

chapters.title: Protocol
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Flashback-threaded chapter tracing how the unnamed embassy recruits men like him — men with no families, no records, no exits. Jonah realizes the protocol has no clause for what happens when the agency itself is the threat. Beat: grief for the self he surrendered.

chapters.title: Forty Hours
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Jonah/Amara. They trace the insurance shell company to a director who is also on the embassy's payroll. Voss sends a cleanup team; Jonah barely extracts Amara from a safehouse ambush. Beat: adrenaline giving way to the terrifying intimacy of trusting someone with your life.

chapters.title: The Brother
chapters.summary: POV: Amara. To find her brother, Amara trades the server's decryption key to a corrupt police colonel — a betrayal she hides from Jonah. She gets her brother back broken but alive, and learns the attack timeline moved up: six hours before dawn. Beat: guilt braided with relief.

chapters.title: What Voss Knows
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Jonah confronts Voss aboard the extraction flight's ground crew staging area and discovers Voss isn't corrupt — he's terrified. The order came from above Voss, from the founding patron whose fortune the insurance scheme replenishes. Beat: the sick vertigo of realizing the ladder has no top rung.

chapters.title: Refinery Road
chapters.summary: POV: alternating. With five hours left, Jonah and Amara infiltrate the refinery's control systems while hired technicians arm the staged failure. Amara's brother provides the one credential they lack. Beat: quiet resolve — love declared not in words but in who stays behind to hold the door.

chapters.title: Dawn Flight
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Climax. Jonah triggers the safety override as the sabotage initiates, then broadcasts the entire server archive publicly, burning himself and the agency in one act. Voss lets the extraction flight leave empty rather than stop him. Beat: catharsis through sacrifice — survival redefined as witness.

chapters.title: Unwitnessed
chapters.summary: POV: Amara. Weeks later, hearings ripple through ministries while a man with no records and a woman with a suspended career share coffee in Accra. The attack is public knowledge; its preventers are not. Beat: bittersweet peace — power exposed but not destroyed, and a small life chosen deliberately over a large one imposed.
